## X. Political Morality (1862)

On Moran's promotion to be Secretary of the Legation, Mr. Seward offered Minister Adams a choice: would he like the assistant secretaryship for his son? It was the first—and last—office ever formally offered Henry Adams, and both father and son judged it useless. Any young man could make some sort of assistant secretary; only one, just then, could make an assistant son. His position remained irregular, half domestic, half diplomatic, attached by courtesy to the Minister at Court and attached to nothing else at all. As years went on he began to find advantages in this absence of position. Gradually he aspired to become simply a member of society—a gentleman with no official label—and the irregular status lent itself to an irregular education that seemed the only education he would ever get.

Such as it was, few young men had more. In the spring and summer of 1863, Secretary Seward grasped that his representatives abroad needed support beyond mere despatches. Governments dealt with governments, not with private opinion; to move European feeling, American weight must be brought to bear personally. Seward sent over every important American he could lay his hands on—bankers, bishops—who did their quiet work well, though to the outsider the work seemed wasted and the influential classes more indurated than ever. The waste was only apparent; meanwhile it helped education.

The most interesting of these visitors was Thurlow Weed, who came to manage what the private secretary had attempted two years before with boyish ignorance of his own powers. Weed took charge of the press and began, to the amused astonishment of the Legation, by making what they had learned to accept as the invariable mistake of every amateur diplomat: he wrote letters to the *London Times*. Mistake or not, Weed soon had in his hands all the threads of management and did quietly and smoothly all that was to be done.

Thurlow Weed was a complete American education in himself. His mind was naturally strong and beautifully balanced; his temper never seemed ruffled; his manners carried the tradition of Benjamin Franklin's benevolent simplicity. He was the model of political management and patient address, but the trait that most excited a private secretary was his faculty of irresistibly conquering confidence. Of all flowers in the garden of education, confidence was becoming the rarest; yet before Weed went away, young Adams followed him about not merely obediently but with something like affection, much like a little dog.

The effect of power and publicity on men is the aggravation of self—a sort of tumor that ends by killing the victim's sympathies—yet Weed appeared one of those rare immunes. He thought apparently not of himself but of the person he was talking with. He held himself in the background. He grasped power, but not office; he distributed offices by handfuls without caring to take them. He had the instinct of empire: he gave, but he did not receive. When Adams tried to get behind this superiority and educate himself from the stores of Weed's experience, he found the study still more fascinating. Management was an instinct with Weed, an object pursued for its own sake, as one plays cards; he seemed to play with men as if they were only cards, incapable of counting himself one of them. He took them and played them for their face value; but once, after telling—with his usual humor—some strong stories of the Albany lobby, the private secretary made bold to ask outright: "Then, Mr. Weed, do you think that no politician can be trusted?" Weed hesitated for a moment; then said in his mild manner: "I never advise a young man to begin by thinking so."

At the time this lesson translated itself to Adams in a moral sense, as though Weed had said: Youth needs illusions. As he grew older he thought Weed had meant it rather as a question of how the game should be played. Principles had better be left aside; values were enough. Adams knew he could never learn to play politics in so masterly a fashion; his education and his nervous system equally forbade it, though he admired the impersonal faculty of the master who could efface himself and his temper in the game.

The teachings of Weed and of William Evarts—Seward's law counsel, who liked to discuss the same problem in a different key, holding that "the world can absorb only doses of truth; too much would kill it"—were practical, and the private secretary's life turned on their value. He had begun, contrary to Weed's advice, by taking English bad faith for granted. Was he wrong? Whether one was dealing with honest men or rogues altered every calculation.

Thus far the private secretary felt officially sure of dishonesty. The recognition of belligerency, the Trent Affair, the escape of the Alabama in July 1862 despite Solicitor-General Collier's written opinion that it presented "a strong case of infringement of the Foreign Enlistment Act, which, if not enforced on this occasion, is little better than a dead letter"—all pointed the same way. Lord Russell had started in May 1861 with the assumption that the Confederacy was established, every step he took proved persistence in the same idea, and he was waiting only for the proper moment to interpose. With the insolence of youth and zeal, Henry Adams concluded that Earl Russell simply lied; although the Minister thought differently, he had to act as though Russell were false.

Month by month the demonstration followed its stages—one of the most perfect educational courses in diplomacy a young man ever pursued at public expense. The most costly tutors in the world were provided: on the British side, Palmerston, Russell, Westbury, Gladstone, Granville; on the American, Seward, Minister Adams, Evarts, Weed. But there was only one student to profit by this immense staff of teachers.

To the end of his life Adams labored over the lessons then taught. Palmerston wrote to Russell in September 1862, when Lee's invasion of Maryland seemed to threaten Washington itself, suggesting the moment might have come for England and France to recommend separation. Russell's reply—from Gotha, September 17—astonished anyone who had supposed the more impulsive temperament was Palmerston's. Where Palmerston had merely floated a question, Russell answered that the time had come for offering mediation "with a view to the recognition of the independence of the Confederates," and that if mediation failed, England "ought ourselves to recognize the Southern States as an independent State." He proposed a Cabinet meeting for the twenty-third or thirtieth. The roles had been reversed: Russell wrote what was expected from Palmerston, or even more violently; Palmerston replied more temperately.

Russell's course, from first to last, had all the look of rigid determination to break up the Union. His letter of September 17 hung directly on his earlier encouragement of the Alabama and protection of the rebel navy; and the whole policy had its root in the Proclamation of Belligerency of May 13, 1861. Yet Russell obstinately denied any such design and persistently assured Minister Adams of his honest and impartial neutrality.

And then Gladstone intervened, and with a rhapsody that made Russell seem sane and all education superfluous. If one point in the world's politics was fixed, one element serious, it was the British Exchequer; and if one man could be counted on by overwhelming interest to remain within rational bounds, it was the Chancellor of the Exchequer. Gladstone had been educated beyond all record of English training. From him, if from no one else, the poor student could safely learn.

Palmerston notified Gladstone of the proposed intervention and Gladstone replied eagerly, urging speed—citing the rapid advance of Southern arms and the risk of "violent impatience in the cotton-towns of Lancashire." Then, on October 7, after a fortnight's further reflection, having noted in his diary that morning that "Lancashire and America are both critical," Gladstone rose at a great dinner in Newcastle and deliberately pronounced his famous phrase: that Jefferson Davis and the Southern leaders had made an army, were making a navy, and—"what is more than either"—had made a nation.

The old-fashioned logical drama required unity and sense; the actual drama is a pointless puzzle. When the curtain fell on Gladstone's speech, any student had the right to suppose the drama ended. In practice, Palmerston was outraged and immediately put up Sir George Cornewall Lewis to repudiate the Chancellor, while turning the ministerial press against him. Russell, by contrast, if he agreed with Palmerston in anything, followed Gladstone; on October 13 he issued his call for the Cabinet to meet on October 23 to discuss "the duty of Europe to ask both parties to agree to a suspension of arms."

Minister Adams, deeply perturbed, delayed demanding an explanation. When at last he saw Russell on October 23—the very day of the Cabinet meeting—Russell offered what the Minister reported as a "slight indication of embarrassment," denied that Gladstone had intended anything serious by his remarks, and assured Adams that the Government's intention was to adhere to "the rule of perfect neutrality" without "the smallest interference, direct or otherwise." Adams pressed him: was he to understand that no change of policy was now proposed? "To which he gave his assent."

What the Minister never knew—and what his son learned only from Spencer Walpole's official life of Russell, published in 1889—was that Russell, within hours of this categorical assurance, had proposed intervention to the Cabinet and been voted down. Newcastle, Sir George Grey, and Granville had all opposed it. Russell and Gladstone stood nearly alone. "Considerations such as these prevented the matter being pursued any further." Within an hour of that decision—before or after, it hardly mattered—Russell told the United States Minister that no change of policy was proposed, and confirmed it with a direct "Yes."

Gladstone's own diary entries for November 11–13, read forty years later, left the private secretary stupefied: "Lord Russell rather turned tail. He gave way without resolutely fighting out his battle. However, though we decline for the moment, the answer is put upon grounds and in terms which leave the matter very open for the future." The only resolute, conscientious champion of intervention, throughout the whole affair, had been Gladstone.

All the world had been at cross-purposes, had misunderstood themselves and the situation, had known none of the facts. One would have done better to draw no conclusions at all.

The evidence against Gladstone seemed, even after forty years, overwhelming—his Newcastle speech warranted no charitable reading—yet the highest education could reach, in this analysis, only a reduction to the absurd. Nothing a young man could have reached in 1862 would have approached the level that Mr. Gladstone himself admitted in his confessions of 1896:

*I have yet to record an undoubted error, the most singular and palpable, I may add the least excusable of them all, especially since it was committed so late as in the year 1862 when I had outlived half a century... I declared in the heat of the American struggle that Jefferson Davis had made a nation.... Strange to say, this declaration, most unwarrantable to be made by a Minister of the Crown with no authority other than his own, was not due to any feeling of partisanship for the South or hostility to the North.... I really, though most strangely, believed that it was an act of friendliness to all America to recognize that the struggle was virtually at an end.... That my opinion was founded upon a false estimate of the facts was the very least part of my fault. I did not perceive the gross impropriety of such an utterance from a Cabinet Minister of a power allied in blood and language, and bound to loyal neutrality; the case being further exaggerated by the fact that we were already, so to speak, under indictment before the world for not (as was alleged) having strictly enforced the laws of neutrality in the matter of the cruisers. My offence was indeed only a mistake, but one of incredible grossness...*

Long and more than patiently—sympathetically—did the private secretary, forty years afterwards in the twilight of a life of study, read and re-read and reflect upon this confession. His whole theory of conspiracy, of policy, of logic and connection in the affairs of men, resolved itself into "incredible grossness." He felt no rancor, for he had won the game; he was willing to forgive the "incapacity of viewing subjects all round" which had nearly cost him life and fortune. He noted, without irritation, that Gladstone's confession had not alluded to his ardent support of Napoleon's intervention policy—the most incredible act of all.

Politics cannot stop to study psychology. Its methods are rough; its judgments rougher still. All this knowledge would not have affected either the Minister or his son in 1862. If the sum of the matter was that no one could be trusted, the matter was so for every government and every age. The lesson that was supposed to teach discrimination ended by teaching none. The private secretary had set out to learn whether Earl Russell could be trusted, and the education lasted a lifetime without a verdict. He was left, at the end, with a single uncomfortable principle: that in politics, individual judgment dissolves into collective error, and the student who tries hardest to see clearly is the last to know it.
